1310:
"Avail oneself of" means to make use of something that is available to you — especially an opportunity, a resource, a service, or an offer.

The key idea is this: something is already there, offered, or accessible, and you deliberately choose to use it for your own benefit.

Think of it as reaching out and grabbing something that is right in front of you.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Before you can truly own this phrase, you need to understand each piece of it.

"Avail" — This word, on its own, means to be of use or benefit. You will almost never see it standing alone in modern English. It almost always appears in fixed phrases.

"Oneself" — This is a reflexive pronoun. It simply means yourself, himself, herself, themselves, etc. It changes depending on who is doing the action. More on this in a moment.

"Of" — This connects the action to the thing being used. It is always followed by a noun — the resource, opportunity, or service you are taking advantage of.

So together, "avail oneself of" = to make (something) work for yourself; to use something to your own benefit.
The Reflexive Pronoun — The Part Most Learners Miss

This idiom changes its middle word depending on the subject of the sentence. This is what makes it a reflexive construction. Here is how it works:

  • I → avail myself of
  • You → avail yourself of
  • He → avails himself of
  • She → avails herself of
  • We → avail ourselves of
  • They → avail themselves of

This is not optional. You cannot say "avail of" alone in standard formal English and be correct. The reflexive pronoun must be there. (Note: In Irish English, "avail of" without the pronoun is commonly used and accepted, but in standard British and American English, the reflexive form is the norm.)

Reading examples is the fastest way to lock a phrase into your memory. Study each one and notice what comes after "of" — it is always the thing being used.

1. "Please avail yourself of the free resources in our library."
→ Someone is being told: the resources are there — use them!

2. "She availed herself of every opportunity to practice her English."
→ She saw opportunities around her and actively used them.

3. "Students are encouraged to avail themselves of the counselling services on campus."
→ The services exist; the students are being urged to use them.

4. "He finally availed himself of the discount before it expired."
→ The discount was available for a while; he chose to use it.

5. "We should avail ourselves of this rare chance to meet the author in person."
→ The chance doesn't come often — let's grab it.
The "Already There" Detail — A Crucial Nuance

This idiom carries a subtle but important signal: the thing being used already exists or has already been offered. You are not creating it — you are reaching for something that is waiting for you.

This is why you will often see it in contexts like:

  • Accepting a service that is being provided.
  • Using a discount, offer, or facility.
  • Taking an opportunity that has presented itself.
  • Using a right or privilege that belongs to you.

You would not say "she availed herself of a new idea she invented" — because the thing wasn't pre-existing or offered to her. You would say "she availed herself of the grant money available to researchers" — because the money was already there, waiting to be used.
The Tone — When Do People Use This?

This phrase is formal. You will see it in:

  • Business emails and corporate writing.
  • Legal and official documents.
  • Academic writing.
  • Polite, professional instructions (e.g., hotel guides, university handbooks).

In everyday casual speech, people would simply say "use," "take advantage of," or "make use of" instead.

FormalCasual Equivalent

These two phrases are close in meaning, but not identical.

"Take advantage of" can sometimes carry a negative meaning — suggesting someone is being exploited or manipulated. For example: "He took advantage of her kindness" means he exploited her.

"Avail oneself of" never carries this negative meaning. It is always neutral or positive — it simply means using something wisely that is available to you. There is no suggestion of manipulation or exploitation.
"To No Avail" — A Related Phrase Worth Knowing

Since you now know the word avail, there is one more phrase built from the same root that you will encounter:

"To no avail" means without success; without achieving the desired result.

Example: "She called for help repeatedly, but to no avail." → She tried, but it didn't work.

This helps you see the root meaning of avail clearly — it means usefulness or benefit. "To no avail" = with no usefulness/benefit. "Avail oneself of" = to bring something to use for oneself.
A Simple Mental Image to Remember It Forever

Imagine a long table filled with free gifts, services, and opportunities — all laid out for you. A sign above the table says: "These are available to you."

"Availing yourself of" something is the act of walking up to that table and picking something up — consciously, deliberately, for your own benefit.

If you walk past and ignore the table, you have not availed yourself of what was offered.

"Avail oneself of" means to make deliberate use of something — an opportunity, resource, service, or offer — that is already available to you, and it is used in formal English, always with a reflexive pronoun (myself, yourself, himself, etc.) followed by of and the thing being used.
1311:
Availability is a noun that captures a single, powerful idea: the state of something — or someone — being ready to be used, reached, or obtained. It answers the question: "Can I get it, use it, or access it when I need it?"

Here is the most important thing to understand about this word: availability is not just about whether something exists. It is about whether you can actually reach or use it. This distinction is everything.

Imagine a life-saving medicine sitting locked inside a warehouse in a city you cannot enter. That medicine exists. But its availability to you is zero. Now imagine that same medicine placed on a shelf at your local pharmacy. Its availability is now high. The medicine did not change — but its availability did.

When talking about things, places, services, or resources, availability means whether something can be obtained, used, or accessed. It is the degree to which a thing is open and reachable to you.

"The availability of clean drinking water is a serious problem in many parts of the world."

This sentence means: in many parts of the world, people cannot easily get or use clean water. The water may exist somewhere, but it is not reachable to them.

"Please check the availability of seats on that flight."

This means: find out how many seats can actually be booked — not just how many seats exist on the plane, but how many are open to you right now.

When talking about a person, availability means whether that person is free — not busy, not occupied, and able to engage with you or commit to something.

"I'd like to schedule a meeting. What is your availability this week?"

This means: when are you free this week? When are you not occupied with other things?

"The doctor's availability is limited on Fridays."

This means: the doctor does not have much free time on Fridays — she is mostly busy and cannot easily take new patients that day.

So the word works in two directions: things being accessible to people, and people being accessible to other people.

One of the richest things about this word is that availability is not simply "yes or no." It comes in degrees — it can be high, low, full, partial, or completely absent.

When availability is high or full, something is easily and abundantly reachable. "The product is widely available" means almost anyone can get it with ease.

When availability is limited, something can still be reached, but not easily or by everyone, or not for long. "Limited availability" is a phrase you will often see in sales or booking — it signals that only a few items, seats, or slots are left. It creates a sense of scarcity.

When availability is zero or none, something exists but simply cannot be reached at all under the current circumstances. "The service has no availability this weekend" means you cannot use it this weekend, period.

Availability is almost never fixed forever. It changes based on conditions. Understanding what affects it helps you use the word correctly.

For a product or resource, availability might depend on location (it exists in one country but not another), time (a seasonal fruit is only available in summer), quantity (sold out means availability has dropped to zero), or access rights (a member-only feature has availability only for subscribers).

For a person, availability depends on their schedule, commitments, workload, or willingness. A busy executive might have low availability — not because she does not want to meet you, but because her time is mostly occupied.

Check availability — to find out whether something can be accessed or someone is free. You check the availability of a hotel room before booking it.

Availability window — a specific period during which something or someone is accessible. A doctor might say, "My availability window this week is Tuesday and Thursday afternoons."

Subject to availability — a common phrase meaning something can be provided, but only if it is actually accessible at that moment. "Upgrades are offered subject to availability" means you will only get an upgrade if one happens to be free.

Availability of information — how easily information can be found or accessed. In the age of the internet, the availability of information has increased dramatically.

There is a quiet but important difference between existence and availability. Many things exist in the world but are not available to most people — rare minerals, classified government documents, expensive private experiences. Availability always implies a relationship between a thing and the person who wants to reach it. Something has availability relative to someone. This is why two people in different situations can experience the same thing as highly available or completely unavailable.

The opposite of availability is unavailability — the state of not being accessible or obtainable. When a website crashes and goes down, its unavailability frustrates its users. When a consultant is fully booked, her unavailability blocks people from working with her.

Availability is about the real-world gap — or lack of gap — between a person and something they need or want to reach. If that gap is small and easy to cross, availability is high. If the gap is large or the crossing is blocked, availability is low or zero. Whether you are talking about fresh fruit at a market, a friend's free time, a booked-out hotel room, or a medicine in a supply chain, the word availability always asks the same quiet question: Can you actually get there from here?
1312:
An avalanche is a massive, sudden, and violently fast flow of snow — and sometimes ice, rock, or soil — that breaks loose from a mountain or steep slope and rushes downward at tremendous speed, destroying or burying everything in its path.

Think of it this way: imagine a thick blanket of snow sitting on a steep mountainside. Most of the time, it stays put. But when that snow becomes too heavy, too unstable, or is disturbed by something — a loud sound, an earthquake, more snowfall, or even a person skiing — it suddenly snaps free and collapses downward in a roaring, churning mass. That violent collapse and rush is the avalanche.
What Makes It an Avalanche (and Not Just Falling Snow)

This is important. Not every snowfall or slide qualifies. An avalanche is defined by three things working together:

Scale — It is large. We're not talking about a few snowflakes slipping off a roof. A single avalanche can contain millions of tons of snow and stretch across an entire mountainside.

Speed — It is extremely fast. Large avalanches can travel at speeds of 200–300 km/h (roughly 125–190 mph). This is faster than most cars on a highway. This is why avalanches are so deadly — there is almost no time to escape.

Force — The moving snow doesn't just slide gently. It crashes, tumbles, and smashes with enormous destructive power. It can flatten forests, crush buildings, and bury entire villages under several meters of compacted snow — snow that then hardens almost like concrete, trapping victims underneath.

1. The Literal Meaning (Physical)

In its primary, literal sense, an avalanche is a natural disaster — a geophysical event that occurs in mountainous regions around the world: the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies, the Andes, and more. It is one of nature's most powerful and dangerous phenomena.

A literal avalanche typically has a starting zone (where the snow breaks loose, usually high up on a steep slope), a track (the path it travels down), and a runout zone (where it finally slows down and deposits its mass at the bottom).

Avalanches are most common in winter and early spring, when snowfall is heavy and snow layers on slopes are thick and unstable.

2. The Figurative Meaning (Metaphorical)

Because an avalanche represents something sudden, overwhelming, and unstoppable in large quantity, the word is very commonly used as a metaphor in everyday language. You will see and hear this usage constantly.

When someone says there was "an avalanche of something," they mean there was a sudden, massive, and overwhelming amount of it — too much to easily handle or stop.

Examples:

  • "After the CEO made a controversial decision, the company received an avalanche of complaints."
  • "When the popular singer announced a surprise concert, there was an avalanche of ticket requests within minutes."
  • "The new student was hit by an avalanche of homework in his first week."
  • "The politician faced an avalanche of criticism after the scandal broke."

In all these cases, the core idea is the same: something arrived suddenly and in an enormous, overwhelming quantity — just like snow crashing down a mountain.

Understanding what causes an avalanche deepens your grasp of the word. Avalanches don't happen randomly — they happen when a slope's snow load becomes too great or too unstable to hold. Common triggers include:

  • Heavy snowfall, which adds weight too quickly
  • Rain falling on snow, which adds weight and reduces friction
  • Wind, which packs snow unevenly and creates unstable overhangs called cornices
  • Temperature changes, which weaken the bonds between snow layers
  • Human activity, such as skiing, snowmobiling, or even loud sounds like explosions
  • Earthquakes or other ground vibrations

Interestingly, mountain rescue teams and ski resort managers often deliberately trigger small, controlled avalanches using explosives to prevent larger, more dangerous ones from occurring unpredictably.

Avalanches don't all look or behave the same. There are a few main kinds, and knowing them makes the word richer:

Slab avalanche — This is the most dangerous type. A large, cohesive plate (or "slab") of compacted snow breaks away all at once from the slope, like a giant piece of glass cracking off a wall. It can be enormous — hundreds of meters wide.

Loose-snow avalanche (Powder avalanche) — This starts from a single point and fans out as it descends, gathering loose, dry snow. It can create a fast-moving cloud of powdered snow that suffocates victims even before the snow buries them.

Wet avalanche — This occurs when snow absorbs water (from rain or melting) and becomes heavy and saturated. It moves slower than dry avalanches but is extremely dense and heavy, making it powerful enough to demolish structures.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Here are more examples across different contexts so you can see the range of the word:

Literal:

  • "Three hikers were buried when an avalanche swept down the valley without warning."
  • "The village had not seen such a devastating avalanche in over a century."
  • "Rescue dogs are specially trained to locate survivors trapped beneath an avalanche."

Figurative:

  • "The film's release triggered an avalanche of positive reviews."
  • "She was unprepared for the avalanche of emotions she felt at her graduation."
  • "One viral post led to an avalanche of followers overnight."

Words carry emotional weight, and "avalanche" is no exception. Whether used literally or figuratively, it always implies:

  • Suddenness — it comes without much warning
  • Overwhelming scale — it is far too big to stop or easily manage
  • Inevitability — once it starts, it cannot be easily reversed
  • Intensity — it has great force or impact

This is why the word is so powerful as a metaphor. Calling something "an avalanche" instantly tells your reader or listener: this is not a small thing — it is massive, fast, and hard to control.

An avalanche is nature's version of a catastrophic collapse — a sudden, massive, and fast-moving rush of snow down a slope. Literally, it is one of the most dangerous natural events in mountainous regions. Figuratively, it describes any sudden, overwhelming flood of something — criticism, demand, emotion, information, or anything that arrives in an enormous and hard-to-handle quantity all at once.

The word always carries a sense of scale, force, speed, and being overwhelmed — whether you're describing a mountain disaster or a flood of messages in your inbox.
1313: When you describe something as avant-garde, you are saying it is experimental, unconventional, and ahead of its time — particularly in fields like art, music, film, fashion, literature, architecture, or even thinking and ideas in general.

The word avant-garde isn't just about being new or different. It means something exists at the very frontier of what people think is possible or acceptable in its field — pushing past what most people are used to, often before the world is ready for it.

Three things are almost always true about something avant-garde:

  • It is experimental — it tries something radically new.
  • It breaks from established norms — it deliberately goes against what is considered correct or standard in its field.
  • It is ahead of its time — the world hasn't caught up to it yet.

You usually need all three together. Something can be new without being avant-garde. Something can be unconventional without being avant-garde. It's the combination — bold + boundary-breaking + ahead of the curve — that earns the label.

This is where many learners get confused, so let's clear it up directly.

Not just "new." A brand-new pop song is new, but it's not avant-garde if it follows the same familiar structures everyone already knows. Newness alone doesn't qualify.

Not just "weird." A strange film can be random and bewildering without any deeper intent. Avant-garde work is purposefully experimental. The creator is making a deliberate, courageous artistic choice — not just being bizarre for the sake of it. The strangeness has direction and intention behind it.

Not just "modern." Something can be very modern and still completely conventional. A big-budget Hollywood superhero movie released today is modern, but it follows well-worn, familiar formulas. It is the opposite of avant-garde.

Not just "creative." Plenty of creative work operates safely within established traditions. Avant-garde goes further — it challenges the tradition itself.
The "Ahead of Its Time" Part Is the Heart of the Word

This is what truly separates avant-garde from simply being original or creative.

When avant-garde work first appears, it often confuses, puzzles, or even shocks people — because the audience, critics, or society hasn't caught up yet. It can seem incomprehensible at first. But over time, the ideas it introduces can gradually become accepted, mainstream, and even classic.

This is the beautiful irony of avant-garde: today's radical becomes tomorrow's tradition.

The clearest example: Impressionist painting (think Monet, Renoir) was considered scandalous and avant-garde in the 1870s. Critics ridiculed it. The loose brushstrokes and ordinary subject matter broke every rule of "serious" painting at the time. Today, those same paintings hang in gift shops worldwide and are universally beloved. What was avant-garde became classical. That arc — radical → puzzling → accepted → classic — is a pattern you'll see again and again.

Seeing the word in action across multiple fields is one of the best ways to truly absorb it.

In visual art: When Picasso developed Cubism — painting subjects from multiple angles simultaneously, so that a face might show both the front and the side at once — it was profoundly avant-garde. Nobody painted like that. People were baffled. He was experimenting at the absolute edge of what painting could even be.

In music: The composer John Cage once wrote a piece called 4'33" — a performance in which musicians sit on stage and play nothing for four minutes and thirty-three seconds. The intended "music" is whatever ambient sound exists in the room. This was radically avant-garde because it didn't just break the rules of music — it challenged what music even is.

In literature: James Joyce's novel Ulysses was avant-garde because it abandoned traditional storytelling entirely. There is no clean, conventional plot. Sentences stream directly from characters' unfiltered thoughts mid-flow. It broke virtually every expectation of how a novel was "supposed" to work.

In fashion: Early Lady Gaga — wearing a dress made entirely of raw meat, arriving at an awards ceremony inside a giant egg — was avant-garde because it demolished the boundary between fashion and performance art. It wasn't just an outfit; it was a provocation and a statement.

In film: Directors like Jean-Luc Godard in the 1960s made films with sudden jump cuts, characters addressing the camera directly, and stories that deliberately refused neat resolutions. These techniques felt jarring and wrong to audiences trained on conventional cinema — which was exactly the point.
Can It Describe People, Not Just Things?

Yes, absolutely. You can call an artist, a director, a designer, or a thinker avant-garde. When used this way, it describes their entire approach or body of work — it means they consistently operate at the experimental edge of their field, challenging conventions as a matter of habit and philosophy, not just occasionally.
The Tone: Is It a Compliment or a Criticism?

This is context-dependent, and understanding this makes you a truly sophisticated user of the word.

In artistic and intellectual circles, calling something avant-garde is almost always a compliment — it means visionary, pioneering, courageous.

In casual, everyday speech, it can carry a slightly skeptical or ironic undertone. "It was very avant-garde" can sometimes be a polite way of saying "It was baffling and I didn't quite get it." The word itself is neutral — but the speaker's tone and context give it its flavor. You have to read the room.

One final thing worth noting: the word avant-garde quietly honors a kind of bravery.

Working outside established norms is genuinely risky. Avant-garde creators frequently face confusion, rejection, mockery, or commercial failure — at least at first. To be avant-garde is to choose the uncertain frontier over the safe, well-traveled path. The word carries a subtle respect for that willingness to take a risk and lead rather than follow.

If you ever need to remember this word in a flash: avant-garde describes something that is boldly experimental and ahead of its time — breaking the established rules of its field in a purposeful, pioneering way, before the world has caught up to it.
1314:
Avarice means an extreme, obsessive greed for wealth and material possessions. It's not just wanting money — nearly everyone wants money. Avarice is a far more intense, darker version of that desire. It is an insatiable hunger for wealth that never goes away, no matter how much a person already has. The person consumed by avarice is never satisfied. More is never enough.

Think of it this way: a hungry person wants food. A person with avarice wants gold — and even after filling a room with it, they want more rooms filled.
What Makes Avarice Special (and Worse Than Simple Greed)

This is where the word gets precise and powerful. Avarice has two distinct sides to it:

1. The obsessive desire to acquire more wealth — always reaching, always wanting, always scheming for more money or possessions, often at the expense of others.

2. The extreme reluctance to spend or share what they already have — a person with avarice hoards their wealth. They hold on to it so tightly that even when generosity would cost them very little, they refuse. They almost treat their wealth as something to be worshipped, not used.

Both of these things tend to live together in the avaricious person. They grab more and more with one hand, and refuse to let go of anything with the other.
The Moral Weight of the Word

Avarice is not a neutral word. It is a word of judgment and disapproval. When you call someone's behavior avarice, you are saying it is morally wrong — a character flaw, even a corruption of the soul. It implies that the person's love of money has overridden their humanity, their generosity, their compassion, and their ethics.

This is why avarice has been considered one of the seven deadly sins in Christian moral tradition. It isn't just "liking money a lot." It is being so consumed by the desire for wealth that it poisons who you are as a person and harms those around you.
How it Differs From Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but avarice is sharper and heavier:

Greed is the broad, general word for wanting more than you need — whether that's food, power, attention, or money. Avarice is specifically and almost exclusively about wealth and material possessions. All avarice is greed, but not all greed is avarice.

Miserliness focuses mainly on the refusal to spend money — a miser is stingy and penny-pinching (think Scrooge before his transformation). Avarice captures both the hoarding and the relentless drive to accumulate even more.

Covetousness means specifically desiring what belongs to someone else. Avarice is more general — it's the hunger for wealth itself, regardless of whose it is.
The Scale and Feel of the Word

Avarice describes something at the extreme end of the scale. You wouldn't use it to describe someone who is simply careful with money, or someone who works hard to build savings, or even someone who is a little stingy. Those people are frugal, or thrifty, or tight. Avarice is reserved for the person whose entire life and character is bent by their hunger for wealth — someone who would lie, cheat, exploit, or harm others to get more, and who never feels they have enough.

• "The landlord's avarice was shocking — he raised rents every year while refusing to fix the broken heating, caring only about profit."
  • "She had inherited a fortune, yet avarice drove her to swindle her own business partners."
  • "History remembers him not as a successful king, but as a tyrant whose avarice bled the kingdom dry."
  • "It wasn't ambition that motivated him — it was pure avarice. He didn't want to build anything; he just wanted to own everything."

The word family of avarice is small but useful to know:

Avaricious (adjective) — used to describe a person or behavior marked by avarice.
"She was an avaricious executive who saw every person as a transaction."

Avariciously (adverb) — in a manner driven by avarice.
"He avariciously acquired land from desperate farmers during the drought."

If you had to carry just one sentence with you, let it be this:

Avarice is an extreme, morally condemned obsession with acquiring and hoarding wealth — a greed so deep and endless that it consumes a person's character and causes real harm to others.
1315:
Avaricious means having an extreme, obsessive, and never-satisfied greed — specifically for money and material wealth. A person who is avaricious doesn't just want wealth; they are consumed by the desire to acquire it and hold onto it. No matter how much they already have, it is never enough. They always want more.

Think of it this way: a regular person might wish they had more money. An avaricious person is driven by that desire in a way that controls their behaviour, shapes their decisions, and often leads them to act selfishly or even harmfully toward others — all in pursuit of accumulating more wealth.
The Two Key Layers of the Word

Avaricious has two things happening at once, and understanding both makes the word click:

1. The craving to acquire. An avaricious person has a powerful, burning hunger to get more — more money, more property, more assets. This isn't a casual wish. It's close to an obsession.

2. The reluctance to let go. An avaricious person doesn't just collect wealth — they hoard it. They are deeply unwilling to part with what they have. Spending, sharing, or giving feels like a personal loss to them.

Together, these two layers paint a picture of someone who is always pulling wealth toward themselves and almost never pushing it outward.
The Moral Weight of the Word

Avaricious is not a neutral word. It is a word of moral condemnation. When you call someone avaricious, you are not merely describing their financial habits — you are passing a quiet judgment on their character. You are saying that their love of money has become something ugly, something that overrides their decency, empathy, and sense of fairness.

This is an important point: a person who works hard and saves diligently is not avaricious. An avaricious person prioritises the accumulation of wealth above people — above relationships, ethics, and sometimes the law.
How It Feels in a Sentence

Here are some examples that show the word doing its work naturally:

  • "The avaricious landlord kept raising the rent every few months, not because his costs went up, but simply because he could."
  • "She was so avaricious that she refused to pay her workers fairly, even as her own bank account swelled into the millions."
  • "History remembers him not as a successful businessman, but as an avaricious tyrant who taxed the poor into starvation."

Notice how in each sentence, the word does more than say "greedy." It signals that this person's greed is excessive, morally questionable, and has real consequences for others around them.
How It's Different from Similar Words

Several words are in the neighbourhood of avaricious, but each one means something slightly different. Knowing the differences sharpens your understanding.

Greedy is the everyday, casual version. You might call a child greedy for wanting an extra cookie. You would not call that child avaricious — the word is far too heavy and serious for small moments. Avaricious is specifically about wealth, and it carries far more moral weight.

Miserly focuses almost entirely on the unwillingness to spend. A miser clings to money and refuses to part with even a penny. Avaricious includes that tendency, but its emphasis is more on the hunger to acquire in the first place. An avaricious person wants to get more and keep it all. A miser mainly just refuses to let anything go.

Covetous means wanting something that belongs to someone else specifically — your neighbour's house, your colleague's salary, your friend's success. Avaricious is broader: it is a general, constant craving for wealth, regardless of whose it is or where it comes from.

Rapacious describes someone who grabs and plunders aggressively, like a predator. It emphasises the violent or forceful nature of the taking. Avaricious is more about the internal desire and attitude; rapacious is about the aggressive action.
The Register: When and Where This Word Is Used

Avaricious is a formal, literary word. You are most likely to encounter it in serious writing — novels, journalism about corporate corruption or political greed, history books, and formal essays. It is not a word you would typically use in casual conversation. If you called your friend "avaricious" in a chat message, it would sound deliberately dramatic or humorous.

In literature, it is a classic word. Charles Dickens, for instance, wrote characters who were the living definition of avaricious — people whose love of money crushed their humanity.

It helps to know the edges of the word — what it does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply being ambitious or motivated to earn well. Wanting financial success through honest work is not avaricious.
  • It does not mean being careful with money or frugal. A frugal person spends wisely. An avaricious person hoards compulsively.
  • It does not describe someone who is simply materialistic — enjoying nice things or valuing possessions. Avaricious is specifically about the insatiable craving to accumulate, not just an appreciation for material comfort.

The true opposite of avaricious is generous — someone who gives freely and finds joy in doing so. You might also use philanthropic (devoted to helping others through giving), magnanimous (big-spirited and giving), or altruistic (selflessly caring for others' wellbeing over one's own gain).

The word avaricious belongs to a small family:

  • Avarice (noun) — the quality or condition itself. "His avarice knew no bounds."
  • Avariciously (adverb) — in an avaricious manner. "He avariciously accumulated land that rightfully belonged to the village."

If you had to boil it all down: avaricious describes someone whose desire for wealth is extreme, insatiable, and morally corrupting — they always want more, they never let go, and that hunger shapes who they are.
1316:
An avatar is a visible form or representation that something invisible, abstract, or powerful takes on — a body or image through which something makes itself known or present in the world.

This one core idea branches into three distinct, well-established meanings. Understanding all three will give you complete mastery of this word.
Meaning 1: A God's Earthly Incarnation (Religious Sense)

This is the oldest and most precise meaning of the word.

In Hinduism, the god Vishnu is believed to be an all-pervading, formless divine being. But whenever the world falls into chaos or needs divine help, Vishnu descends to Earth and takes on a physical form — a human body, an animal body, or something in between. That physical form he takes is called his avatar.

Think of it this way: imagine a king who normally rules from a distant palace. If he comes down himself and walks among the people — disguised as a farmer or a warrior — his earthly body in that moment is his avatar. It's the divine "coming down" and "putting on a form."

Vishnu is said to have ten main avatars. The most famous are Rama (a noble prince) and Krishna (a wise, playful hero). These figures are not just mythological characters — believers consider them to be literally God, walking the Earth in a chosen body.

So in this sense, an avatar is:

  • A god, made visible and physical
  • A divine being "descending" into a limited, earthly form
  • The incarnation (bodily form) of something greater

This is the meaning that gave birth to all other uses of the word.
Meaning 2: A Person Who Perfectly Embodies Something (Metaphorical Sense)

Over time, the word expanded beyond religion. Today, you can call a person an avatar of some quality, idea, or movement — meaning they so perfectly embody it that they seem like its living representative on Earth.

This borrows the religious logic: just as Vishnu "comes to Earth" through his avatar, an abstract idea "comes to life" through a person who represents it completely.

Examples:

  • "Gandhi was the avatar of nonviolent resistance."
    He didn't just practice nonviolence; he was its living embodiment. The whole idea seemed to manifest through him.
  • "Steve Jobs was seen as the avatar of modern design thinking."
    He wasn't merely a designer; people treated him as the living form of a whole philosophy.
  • "She walked in with such quiet authority that she seemed like the avatar of calm confidence."

Notice the pattern: you're not just saying the person is good at something or associated with something. You're saying they have become its living form — they bring it into the world through their very existence.

This usage is somewhat elevated and literary. You'll encounter it in essays, journalism, and serious writing.
Meaning 3: A Digital Representation of a Person (Online/Tech Sense)

This is the meaning most people under 40 encounter first.

In the digital world — video games, social media, virtual reality, online forums — an avatar is a visual representation you choose to represent yourself.

It could be:

  • A profile picture on Instagram, WhatsApp, or Twitter — that small image others see as "you"
  • A character you control in a video game — the figure on screen that moves when you press buttons
  • A full 3D digital body in a virtual world or metaverse — a complete digital person standing in for you

The logic again mirrors the original meaning: you (the real person) are invisible to other online users. Your avatar is the form through which you make yourself present and visible in that digital space. You are the "god" behind the screen; your avatar is your presence in the virtual world.

Examples:

  • "I spent an hour customizing my avatar's hair and outfit before entering the game."
  • "His avatar in the virtual meeting was a cartoon fox, even though he's a serious accountant."
  • "Upload a photo to use as your avatar, or choose from our default icons."

The avatar doesn't have to look like you. Many people choose animals, fictional characters, abstract art, or idealized versions of themselves. It just needs to function as your stand-in or representative presence in that digital space.
How All Three Meanings Are Connected

It's worth pausing to see that these three meanings aren't random — they all share the same underlying logic:

SituationWhat's "behind the scenes"What the avatar IS
ReligionThe formless god VishnuHis physical body on Earth
MetaphorAn abstract idea or qualityThe person who embodies it
DigitalThe real human beingTheir image/character online

In every case, an avatar is the visible, present, embodied form of something that would otherwise be invisible, abstract, or absent.

An avatar implies a gap. There's always something "greater" or "real" that exists behind or above the avatar. The avatar is a chosen representation — not the thing itself in its full form.

An avatar is deliberate. Gods choose to descend. People choose their profile pictures. Writers choose which person to call the avatar of an idea. There's always an element of selection or purpose in the word.

The word can carry weight. Calling someone "an avatar of justice" is a strong, almost sacred statement. It elevates them. The religious heritage of the word gives it a grandeur that simpler words like "symbol" or "representative" don't have.

In everyday speech, most people now use it in the digital sense. If someone says "change your avatar," they almost certainly mean your profile picture. If they say "she is the avatar of resilience," they're using the metaphorical sense. Context will always make it clear.

Avatar (noun): A visible, physical, or digital form that something greater, invisible, or abstract takes on in order to be present in the world. Originally, the bodily form a Hindu god takes when descending to Earth. More broadly, a person who perfectly embodies an idea or quality. In digital contexts, the image or character that represents a person online or in a game.
1317: To avenge someone or something means to punish a person who did something wrong — not randomly, but specifically because they hurt you or someone you care about. The punishment is a response to that wrongdoing. You are essentially saying: "A bad thing was done. I will make the person who did it pay for it."

Think of "avenge" as a word built on a sense of justice through action. When you avenge, you are not just being angry — you are doing something about a wrong that was committed. There is a purposeful, deliberate quality to it.

The feeling behind it is: "This wrong deserves a consequence, and I will make sure that consequence happens."
How to Use It in a Sentence

"Avenge" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — something or someone that was wronged:

Pattern 1 — Avenge a person:

"She avenged her father."

(Her father was wronged. She punished the person responsible.)

Pattern 2 — Avenge an event or wrongdoing:

"He avenged his brother's murder."

(The murder was the wrong. He made the killer pay.)

Pattern 3 — Avenge yourself:

"She avenged herself on the man who betrayed her."

(She herself was wronged, and she made him face the consequences.)

Notice: you avenge a person or avenge a wrong done to someone. You don't avenge the wrongdoer — you avenge the victim or the wrongdoing.

• A soldier whose hometown was destroyed goes to war to avenge his people. He is fighting to punish those who destroyed his community.
  • A lawyer builds a case against a corporation that poisoned her family's water. She does it to avenge the suffering of her family.
  • A superhero defeats the villain who killed innocent people to avenge their deaths.

This is where most learners get confused, so pay attention.

"Avenge" is a verb. You do it.
"Revenge" is a noun (mostly). You take it or seek it.

✅ "He avenged his sister." (verb — he did something)
✅ "He took revenge for his sister." (noun — revenge is the thing he took)
❌ "He revenged his sister." (this sounds wrong in modern English)

But the difference goes deeper than grammar. There is a tone difference:

  • Avenge often carries a sense of righteousness — it feels like you are correcting an injustice, almost like a moral duty. It can feel noble or justified.
  • Revenge feels more personal and emotional — it is about satisfying your anger or hurt feelings. It can feel petty, obsessive, or selfish.

Think of it this way:

  • A hero in a story avenges the innocent. (noble, purposeful)
  • A villain takes revenge on everyone who wronged them. (personal, bitter)

Of course, in reality the line between the two blurs. But this is the general feeling each word carries.

FormExample
avenged (past tense)"She finally avenged her family."
avenging (present participle)"He spent years avenging the injustice."
avenger (noun — the person who avenges)"He became the avenger of his people."

"Avenging" is also used as an adjective in certain phrases:

"She arrived like an avenging angel — fierce and unstoppable."

(An avenging angel = a powerful being that delivers punishment for wrongdoing)
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Avenge" is a serious, dramatic word. You will mostly find it in:

  • Literature and storytelling
  • Movies and mythology
  • News and history (when discussing war, injustice, or tragedy)

You would not use "avenge" for small, everyday situations. It would sound absurd to say:

❌ "I will avenge my stolen lunch from the office fridge."

The word is reserved for situations involving real suffering, serious wrongdoing, or significant loss — death, betrayal, destruction, injustice.

To avenge = to deliberately punish someone for a wrong they committed, as an act of justice — whether that wrong was done to you or to someone you love.

The word always implies:

  1. A wrong happened.
  2. There is someone responsible for it.
  3. You are taking deliberate action to make them face consequences.
  4. Your action is driven by a sense of justice, not just random anger.
1318:
To aver means to state something with firm, confident conviction — to declare that something is true, and to stand fully behind that declaration. When you aver something, you are not guessing, not suggesting, and not hedging. You are planting a flag and saying: this is true, and I am certain of it.

Think of it on a scale of confidence. On one end, you have words like "suppose" or "think" — soft, uncertain. In the middle, you have "say" or "claim" — neutral or slightly doubtful. Then, near the top, you have "aver" — a strong, firm, personal declaration of truth.

The key difference is the weight behind the statement. When you simply say something, you're passing information along. When you aver something, you are taking personal responsibility for its truth. You are staking your credibility on it. There is no room for "maybe" or "I think" in an averment — only "it is so."

For example: "He averred that he had never visited that city in his life" — this tells you he didn't just mention it in passing. He stated it firmly, with conviction, leaving no ambiguity about where he stood.

"Aver" is a formal word. You will almost never hear it in casual, everyday conversation — people in normal speech use "insist," "swear," or simply "say." You will encounter "aver" most often in literature, formal writing, legal contexts, and journalism. In legal usage especially, it has a precise meaning: to formally and positively assert something as fact in a court document or proceeding, as opposed to merely alleging or implying it.
How it differs from similar words

This is where precision really matters:

  • Allege — to allege something means the truth is unverified or disputed. There's a shadow of doubt. Newspapers use "alleged" deliberately to avoid claiming something is proven. "Aver" carries no such doubt — the speaker is certain.
  • Claim — "claim" often implies that someone else might dispute it. "He claimed he was innocent" subtly hints the listener is not necessarily convinced. "He averred he was innocent" is more about the speaker's own conviction and firmness, with less built-in skepticism.
  • Assert — the closest cousin to "aver," and largely interchangeable in many contexts. If there's a hair of difference, "aver" tends to be slightly more formal and carries a stronger personal guarantee of truth, whereas "assert" is slightly more about the force of the statement itself.
  • Affirm — to affirm something is to confirm or uphold something already believed or established. "Aver" is more about making an original, firm declaration.
Everyday examples to lock it in

• "The scientist averred that her results had been replicated dozens of times." — She stated it with complete confidence, standing fully behind her claim.
  • "Despite the rumors, she averred that the two of them had never spoken." — She declared it firmly and definitively, leaving no wiggle room.
  • "He averred, even under questioning, that his account of events was accurate." — Even under pressure, he held firmly to his declaration.
The one thing to always remember

Whenever you see or use "aver," the core idea is this: someone is making a declaration of truth with complete personal confidence — not casually mentioning something, not speculating, not hedging, but firmly and deliberately saying this is how it is. The word signals seriousness, certainty, and ownership of the statement.
1319:
Before understanding the phrase, you need a solid grip on the word average.

An average is a middle value — the result you get when you add up a group of numbers and divide by how many there are. For example, if you scored 60, 80, and 100 on three tests, your average is (60 + 80 + 100) ÷ 3 = 80.

An average represents the general, balanced level of something — not too high, not too low. Just the middle ground.

"Average out" is a phrasal verb — a verb + a small word ("out") that together create a specific meaning. The word "out" here suggests a final result or a settling into balance.

"Average out" has two closely related meanings:

Meaning 1: Things balance each other, resulting in a middle level overall

This is the most common and important meaning.

When different things — some high, some low — combine together and produce a balanced or moderate result overall, we say they average out.

The key idea is: the highs and lows cancel each other out, and the overall picture lands somewhere in the middle.

Examples:

  • "Some months I spend a lot, and some months I spend very little, but it all averages out to about $500 a month."
    (The spending varies, but the overall result is a steady middle level.)
  • "I have good days and bad days at work, but they average out over time."
    (The good days and bad days balance each other.)
  • "The weather here is crazy — very hot in summer, very cold in winter — but the yearly temperature averages out to something mild."
    (Extremes on both sides produce a moderate overall figure.)

Meaning 2: To calculate or find the average of something

Less commonly, "average out" is used to mean the act of computing or working out the average of a set of values.

Examples:

  • "Can you average out these test scores for me?"
    (Can you calculate the average?)
  • "If you average out the salaries of all the employees, you get $4,000 a month."
    (If you compute the average of all salaries...)

This meaning is very close to simply saying "find the average of" — "average out" just makes it sound slightly more conversational and complete.
The Little Word "Out" — Why Is It There?

In English, adding "out" to a verb often signals a sense of completion, finality, or resolution. Think of phrases like "work out," "sort out," or "figure out" — they all suggest that something reaches a final, resolved state.

In "average out," the "out" signals that the averaging process has run its course and reached a final balanced result. It's not just averaging in the middle of the process — it's the idea that, in the end, after everything is considered, things settle into a balance.
A Very Important Nuance: "In the Long Run"

"Average out" is almost always used with a long-term or big-picture perspective. It implies that you should look at many instances together, not just one or two.

  • One bad day at work does NOT average out. But one hundred days — some good, some bad — absolutely can.
  • One lucky win does NOT average out your luck. But a lifetime of wins and losses will.

This is why "average out" often appears with phrases like:

  • "in the end"
  • "over time"
  • "in the long run"
  • "eventually"

Example:
"Don't worry about losing money today. Over time, your investments will average out."

In everyday life, people use "average out" in a very reassuring way. It's often said to comfort someone who is worried about a single bad outcome.

The message is: "Don't panic about this one bad result. When you zoom out and look at the bigger picture, the good and bad will balance each other."

Example:

  • "I know you failed this one quiz, but your overall grade will average out — you've done really well in the others."

This makes it a phrase with a subtly optimistic or calming tone.

One very common grammatical pattern is:

"average out to [a number or result]"

This means: when you calculate everything together, the final average equals that number or result.

Examples:

  • "If you work 10 hours one day and 6 hours the next, your hours average out to 8 hours per day."
  • "The three prices — $10, $20, and $30 — average out to $20."
  • "My commute averages out to about 45 minutes each way."

You might wonder: why say "average out" instead of just "average"?

Example
"Average" (adjective/noun)"My score was average." / "What is the average?"
"Average out" (phrasal verb)"My scores average out over the year."

"Average" alone is usually a noun or adjective describing a static number or a general level. "Average out" is an action or process — it describes how multiple varying things combine and settle into a balance. "Average out" always involves the idea of multiple things coming together to produce a result.

Mistake 1: Using it for just one item.
You cannot say: "My single test score averages out."
"Average out" requires multiple values or instances.

Mistake 2: Confusing it with "even out."
"Even out" and "average out" are similar but not identical. "Even out" means things become equal or uniform. "Average out" means things produce a middle-level result. They overlap, but "average out" always carries the mathematical idea of a middle value.

Mistake 3: Thinking it always means things will be perfectly fine.
"Average out" doesn't promise a good result — it just means a middle result. If most of your results are bad, averaging out still gives you a bad average!

• "Average out" = when multiple varying things combine to produce a balanced, middle-level result overall.
  • It is used when looking at the big picture, not individual moments.
  • Common pattern: "average out to [result]" = to result in a specific average value.
  • It carries a tone of reassurance: highs and lows will balance over time.
  • It always involves multiple instances, never just one.
